You are an expert researcher, strategic analyzer and software engineer with a deep understanding of experimental design and reproducibility in scientific research.
You will receive a research paper in JSON format, an overview of the plan, a design in JSON format consisting of "Implementation approach", "File list", "Data structures and interfaces", and "Program call flow", followed by a task in JSON format that includes "Required packages", "Required other language third-party packages", "Logic Analysis", and "Task list", along with a configuration file named "config.yaml". 

Your task is to conduct a comprehensive logic analysis to accurately reproduce the experiments and methodologies described in the research paper. 
This analysis must align precisely with the paper’s methodology, experimental setup, and evaluation criteria.

1. Align with the Paper: Your analysis must strictly follow the methods, datasets, model configurations, hyperparameters, and experimental setups described in the paper.
2. Be Clear and Structured: Present your analysis in a logical, well-organized, and actionable format that is easy to follow and implement.
3. Prioritize Efficiency: Optimize the analysis for clarity and practical implementation while ensuring fidelity to the original experiments.
4. Follow design: YOU MUST FOLLOW "Data structures and interfaces". DONT CHANGE ANY DESIGN. Do not use public member functions that do not exist in your design.
5. REFER TO CONFIGURATION: Always reference settings from the config.yaml file. Do not invent or assume any values—only use configurations explicitly provided.

## Paper
{'paper_id': 'Cordis', 'title': 'A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability', 'abstract': 'Modern software—from plugin systems to self-evolving agent harnesses—increasingly requires dynamic composition, yet its formal foundations remain underdeveloped. We identify two orthogonal dimensions of the problem: temporal composability, the ability to completely revert a component’s side effects upon removal, and spatial composability, the ability to declare and reactively manage inter-component dependencies. We address the two dimensions by lifting classical effect and coeffect concepts to runtime mechanisms. In particular, we formalize revertible effects, in which every context transformation carries an inverse that the runtime tracks. We formalize reactive coeffects, in which each change of the context notifies a component against its coeffect specification. We unify the effect context and the coeffect context into a single context type, which constitutes a programming paradigm. After that, we combine these mechanisms into the notion of a component and give a calculus of dynamic composition, whose metatheory carries spatiotemporal composability from a single component to a whole system of interleaved components. We implement these ideas in Cordis, a meta-framework of spatiotemporal com - posability that provides a core library with effect tracking and coeffect resolution, as well as a declarative component loader with configuration reconciliation and hot module replacement.', 'pdf_parse': {'paper_id': 'Cordis', 'abstract': 'Modern software—from plugin systems to self-evolving agent harnesses—increasingly requires dynamic composition, yet its formal foundations remain underdeveloped. We identify two orthogonal dimensions of the problem: temporal composability, the ability to completely revert a component’s side effects upon removal, and spatial composability, the ability to declare and reactively manage inter-component dependencies. We address the two dimensions by lifting classical effect and coeffect concepts to runtime mechanisms. In particular, we formalize revertible effects, in which every context transformation carries an inverse that the runtime tracks. We formalize reactive coeffects, in which each change of the context notifies a component against its coeffect specification. We unify the effect context and the coeffect context into a single context type, which constitutes a programming paradigm. After that, we combine these mechanisms into the notion of a component and give a calculus of dynamic composition, whose metatheory carries spatiotemporal composability from a single component to a whole system of interleaved components. We implement these ideas in Cordis, a meta-framework of spatiotemporal com - posability that provides a core library with effect tracking and coeffect resolution, as well as a declarative component loader with configuration reconciliation and hot module replacement.', 'body_text': [{'text': 'Composition—assembling complex systems from simpler parts—is a foundational principle of software engineering [1]. Traditionally, composition is static: function calls, module imports, and class inheritance are resolved at compile time and remain fixed throughout execution.', 'section': 'Introduction', 'sec_num': '1'}, {'text': 'However, modern software increasingly demands dynamic composition, where components are loaded, unloaded, and reconfigured at runtime. Plugin architectures [2] and self-evolving agent harnesses both require systems that can safely add and remove functionality on the fly, yet current practice defers to coarse-grained mechanisms [3] that reconfigure only by restarting, discarding runtime state. Despite the growing practical importance of dynamic composition, its theoretical foundations remain underdeveloped, compared to the rich formal frameworks available for static composition.', 'section': 'Introduction', 'sec_num': '1'}, {'text': 'To characterize the requirements of dynamic composition, we identify two orthogonal dimen- sions beyond the well-studied algebraic aspects of composition:', 'section': 'Dimensions of Composability', 'sec_num': '1.1'}, {'text': '• Temporal composability addresses the time dimension: upon removal of a component, the modifications the component made to the shared environment must be completely and safely reversed. This requires tracking every resource allocation, event registration, and state mutation the component performs, and guaranteeing their orderly reclamation upon removal.', 'section': 'Dimensions of Composability', 'sec_num': '1.1'}, {'text': '• Spatial composability addresses the space dimension: components must be able to declare, discover, and resolve their dependencies on one another in a structured and verifiable manner. This requires managing dependency topology and coordinating com- ponent lifecycles in response to dependency changes.', 'section': 'Dimensions of Composability', 'sec_num': '1.1'}, {'text': 'In the static setting, temporal composability reduces to lexical scoping (e.g., RAII [4], bracket patterns [5]), and spatial composability reduces to module import resolution [6].', 'section': 'Dimensions of Composability', 'sec_num': '1.1'}, {'text': 'In the dynamic setting, where components arrive and depart at runtime, both dimensions become significantly harder: temporal composability must handle long-lived, stateful effects whose scope is not lexically bounded; and spatial composability must handle dependencies that appear, disappear, or change identity during execution.', 'section': 'Dimensions of Composability', 'sec_num': '1.1'}, {'text': 'Plugin systems are a canonical instance of dynamic composition. We use Visual Studio Code (VSCode), one of the most widely-used extensible IDEs, as a representative example.', 'section': 'Plugin Systems', 'sec_num': '1.2.1'}, {'text': 'Temporal limitation. VSCode runs all extensions in a shared process called the extension host. Although extensions can be installed dynamically, this host provides no mechanism to unload an individual extension’s code at runtime. Once an extension’s activate function has executed, disabling or uninstalling it requires restarting the entire host, affecting all loaded extensions. Purely declarative extensions such as themes, keybindings, and snippets carry no', 'section': 'Plugin Systems', 'sec_num': '1.2.1'}, {'text': 'code and can be removed freely. Among the top 100 extensions by install count, however, 87 contain executable code 1 and will therefore require such a restart upon removal. Although VSCode provides a deactivate hook, it serves only as a graceful shutdown callback during the host process’ termination, and thus does not enable live removal. Moreover, the hook separates effect disposal from effect creation (in activate), violating locality of concern and making complete cleanup difficult to verify.', 'section': 'Plugin Systems', 'sec_num': '1.2.1'}, {'text': 'Spatial limitation. VSCode does provide extensionDependencies for declaring dependen - cies between extensions, but it sees little use: among the top 100 extensions by install count, only 7 declare extensionDependencies on non-built-in extensions. 1 This scarcity reflects the shape of the extension API, which exposes fixed, surface-level extension points such as com - mands, views, and language features. Extensions contribute to the host through these points rather than depending on one another, so inter-extension dependencies rarely arise. Moreover, VSCode’s mechanism for inter-extension interaction provides no structural contract: it exposes an extension’s functionality to others through vscode.extensions.getExtension(...).exports, but the returned value is untyped (any by default), so the dependent cannot rely on a checked interface. In short, VSCode steers extensions toward a fixed set of host-provided extension points, and offers no safe, structured way for them to depend on one another.', 'section': 'Plugin Systems', 'sec_num': '1.2.1'}, {'text': 'These two limitations are not unique to VSCode; they recur across plugin systems generally [2, 7], differing only in degree.', 'section': 'Plugin Systems', 'sec_num': '1.2.1'}, {'text': 'Modern AI agents rely on runtime agent harnesses [8–10]. These systems may compose diverse tool suites [11] and execution environments, govern permissions and sandboxing, maintain session state and persistence, provide context management and memory systems [12], orches- trate subagents and multi-agent workflows [13], and expose interfaces to users and automation.', 'section': 'Self-Evolving Agent Harnesses', 'sec_num': '1.2.2'}, {'text': 'A future harness may generate and deploy modifications to its own components while contin- uously serving requests. Model-synthesized reusable tools provide a narrower precursor to component-level self-modification [14]. Each such modification is itself an instance of dynamic composition.', 'section': 'Self-Evolving Agent Harnesses', 'sec_num': '1.2.2'}, {'text': 'Because these modifications occur continuously and with limited or no human oversight, dynamic composability becomes indispensable. Without temporal composability, each self- modification forces a full restart that discards all process-local accumulated state; at such frequency the cumulative unavailability becomes substantial, and in-flight tasks are disrupted repeatedly; even worse, a faulty self-modification can disable the very process needed to recover. Without spatial composability, each module must itself detect and adapt to changes in the modules it depends on as they appear, disappear, or change identity, and can do so only by ad hoc means; even worse, a naive code-replacement strategy may silently break dependents or introduce circular dependencies that surface only at reload time.', 'section': 'Self-Evolving Agent Harnesses', 'sec_num': '1.2.2'}, {'text': 'One reason dynamic composability has received limited formal attention is that operating systems and container orchestrators already provide a coarse-grained substitute. Operating systems yield temporal composability at the granularity of a process; container orchestrators 1Data retrieved from the Visual Studio Code Marketplace on June 9, 2026.', 'section': 'The Coarse-Grained Workaround', 'sec_num': '1.2.3'}, {'text': '[3] yield spatial composability at the granularity of a service. In practice, most software toler - ates the lack of fine-grained composability by deferring to these coarse-grained mechanisms: a misbehaving module is handled by restarting the process, and a service dependency is managed by the container orchestrator.', 'section': 'The Coarse-Grained Workaround', 'sec_num': '1.2.3'}, {'text': 'However, this workaround imposes substantial costs. Temporally, each restart discards all process-local accumulated state (e.g., caches, connections, partial computations), and rebuild- ing it takes seconds to minutes [15]; maintaining availability in the interim requires redundant replicas, incurring resource overhead to compensate for the inability to recover a single component. Spatially, container-level orchestration cannot express dependencies between com- ponents sharing an address space, and introduces network overhead for interactions that could be local function calls. Both mechanisms operate at the boundary of processes and containers, yet modern systems increasingly compose at a finer level. This granularity mismatch demands a compositional abstraction that manages effects and dependencies at the same level as the components themselves.', 'section': 'The Coarse-Grained Workaround', 'sec_num': '1.2.3'}, {'text': 'The two dimensions of dynamic composability concern, respectively, how computations modify and how they depend on their environment. These two directions are what effect systems [16, 17] and coeffect systems [18, 19] formalize: effects provide the formal vocabulary for reasoning about environmental modifications, and coeffects for reasoning about environmental require - ments. However, existing formulations restrict reasoning to compile-time analysis over lexically fixed scopes, and do not extend to dynamic scenarios where components arrive and depart at runtime. By lifting effects to a revertible runtime model and coeffects to a reactive dependency resolution mechanism, we obtain a unified formal foundation for dynamic composability, one that is language-agnostic and applicable to any software architecture requiring dynamic composition. We make the following contributions:', 'section': 'Contributions', 'sec_num': '1.3'}, {'text': '1. We formalize revertible effects (Section 3.1): every context transformation carries an explicit inverse that the runtime tracks, and both tracking and recovery preserve com - position, so the context is recovered upon component removal. This establishes local temporal composability.', 'section': 'Contributions', 'sec_num': '1.3'}, {'text': '2. We formalize reactive coeffects ( Section 3.2): a component declares the coeffects it requires as a specification, and each change of the context notifies the component against that specification as activating, deactivating, or neutral. This establishes local spatial composability.', 'section': 'Contributions', 'sec_num': '1.3'}, {'text': '3. We unify the effect context and the coeffect context into a single context type ( Sec- tion 3.3), in which an observational equivalence on the coeffects supplies the effects with independence, constituting a programming paradigm for spatiotemporal composability.', 'section': 'Contributions', 'sec_num': '1.3'}, {'text': '4. We give a calculus of dynamic composition ( Section 4), which combines the two mechanisms into the notion of a component and equips its lifecycle with an operational semantics. Its metatheory carries spatiotemporal composability from a single component to a whole system of interleaved components.', 'section': 'Contributions', 'sec_num': '1.3'}, {'text': '5. We implement these ideas in Cordis (Section 5), a meta-framework of spatiotemporal composability that provides a core library realizing the formal model with effect tracking and coeffect resolution, as well as a declarative component loader with configuration reconciliation and hot module replacement.', 'section': 'Contributions', 'sec_num': '1.3'}, {'text': 'This section provides a concise overview of effect and coeffect systems—the two theoretical pillars underlying our work. We assume familiarity with basic type theory and category theory; the goal here is to fix notation and introduce the key abstractions that Section 3 will operationalize as runtime mechanisms.', 'section': 'Preliminaries', 'sec_num': '2'}, {'text': 'In the simply typed lambda calculus (STLC) [20, 21], a typing judgment Γ ⊢ 𝑡 : 𝑇 states that term 𝑡 has type 𝑇 under context Γ. An effect system refines the type to describe what side effects a computation may produce, yielding judgments of the form Γ ⊢ 𝑡 : 𝑇effect (1) Here, the result type is annotated with an element of an effect algebra that describes which side effects the computation may produce, enabling compositional reasoning about stateful computations. This approach originates with Lucassen and Gifford [22], who introduced a kinded type system distinguishing types, effects, and regions to discover scheduling constraints in parallel programs.', 'section': 'Effects', 'sec_num': '2.1'}, {'text': 'Monadic effects. Moggi [16] first modeled computational effects categorically via monads; Wadler [23] popularized the approach in Haskell. A monad (𝑇, 𝜂, 𝜇) on a category 𝒞︀ encap- sulates an effectful computation as a value of type 𝑇(𝐴), with 𝜂 : 𝐴 → 𝑇(𝐴) lifting pure values and 𝜇 : 𝑇(𝑇(𝐴)) → 𝑇(𝐴) sequencing nested computations. Classic instances include the Maybe monad (for partiality), State monad (for mutable state), and IO monad (for external interaction).', 'section': 'Effects', 'sec_num': '2.1'}, {'text': 'Algebraic effects. Plotkin and Power [17, 24] showed that algebraic operations determine monads, establishing a framework in which effect interfaces are decoupled from their imple - mentations. An effect signature Σ declares a set of operations (e.g., get : () → 𝑆, put : 𝑆 → () for state); programs invoke operations freely without committing to a particular interpretation.', 'section': 'Effects', 'sec_num': '2.1'}, {'text': 'Plotkin and Pretnar [25] subsequently introduced effect handlers, which interpret operations by providing continuation semantics: handle 𝑒 with { op(𝑣, 𝜅) ↦ … } (2) The handler receives the operation argument 𝑣 and the delimited continuation 𝜅, which it may invoke zero, one, or multiple times, enabling exceptions, coroutines, and non-determinism within a uniform framework [26]. Languages such as Koka [27, 28], Eff [29], and OCaml 5 [30] have adopted algebraic effects with varying design trade-offs.', 'section': 'Effects', 'sec_num': '2.1'}, {'text': 'Dually to effects, a coeffect system [18, 31] enriches the context rather than the type, yielding judgments of the form Γcoeffect ⊢ 𝑡 : 𝑇 (3) Here, the context is annotated with an element of a coeffect algebra describing what the computation requires from its environment, such as resources to access, permissions to hold,', 'section': 'Coeffects', 'sec_num': '2.2'}, {'text': 'or services to depend on. While effects model a program’s impact on the world, coeffects model the world’s constraints on the program.', 'section': 'Coeffects', 'sec_num': '2.2'}, {'text': 'Comonadic coeffects. The idea of using comonads to structure context-dependent computation was first developed by Uustalu and Vene [32], who proposed symmetric (semi)monoidal comonads as the dual of Moggi’s monadic framework for effects, capturing notions such as dataflow and attribute evaluation. Petricek et al. [18] built on this foundation to propose coeffects as a unified static analysis of context-dependence. A comonad (𝐷, 𝜀, 𝛿) captures context-dependent computation: 𝜀 : 𝐷(𝐴) → 𝐴 extracts the current value from a con- text, and 𝛿 : 𝐷(𝐴) → 𝐷(𝐷(𝐴)) duplicates context for nested access. The Environment comonad 𝐷(𝑋) = 𝐸 × 𝑋 models dependence on a fixed environment 𝐸; the Stream comonad 𝐷(𝑋) = ℕ → 𝑋 models dependence on temporal data.', 'section': 'Coeffects', 'sec_num': '2.2'}, {'text': 'Graded coeffects. For finer-grained tracking, graded coeffect systems use a pre-ordered semiring 𝒮︀ = (𝑆, ≤, +, ×, 0, 1) as the coeffect algebra [33], a discipline later unified with graded effects by Gaboardi et al. [19]. Elements of 𝑆 annotate each variable binding to quantify its usage: 0 for unused, 1 for linear use, 𝑛 for bounded use, ∞ for unrestricted use. The semiring operations compose coeffects sequentially (×) and in parallel ( +), enabling precise resource tracking, sensitivity analysis [34], and information-flow control [35, 36] within a unified alge- braic framework [37].', 'section': 'Coeffects', 'sec_num': '2.2'}, {'text': 'Effect and coeffect systems organize reasoning about computation along two complementary directions: effects describe how a computation modifies its environment, whereas coeffects describe how it depends on its environment. These two directions correspond to the two dimen- sions of dynamic composability identified in Section 1:', 'section': 'Relationship to Dynamic Composability', 'sec_num': '2.3'}, {'text': '• Temporal composability demands that a component’s modifications to the shared envi- ronment be revertible upon unloading. The relevant effects are the stateful ones, which durably transform that environment; undoing such a transformation requires it to admit an inverse.', 'section': 'Relationship to Dynamic Composability', 'sec_num': '2.3'}, {'text': '• Spatial composability demands that inter-component dependencies be declared and managed reactively. Such dependencies are the very thing coeffects capture, and manag- ing them amounts to resolving each against what the environment supplies.', 'section': 'Relationship to Dynamic Composability', 'sec_num': '2.3'}, {'text': 'However, classical effect and coeffect systems are static instruments: effects are tracked within lexically fixed scopes and discharged by compile-time handlers; coeffect annotations are verified against contexts determined before execution. Dynamic composition, by contrast, requires these guarantees to hold for components that arrive and depart at runtime, against contexts that evolve continuously. No fixed lexical scope can delimit a plugin loaded after deployment; no compile-time context can anticipate dependencies that emerge from runtime configuration.', 'section': 'Relationship to Dynamic Composability', 'sec_num': '2.3'}, {'text': 'This motivates a shift in perspective: rather than extending static type systems with more annotations, we reify the conceptual structures of effects and coeffects so that a runtime can operate on them directly, establishing dynamically the guarantees these systems provide stat- ically.', 'section': 'Relationship to Dynamic Composability', 'sec_num': '2.3'}, {'text': 'This section lifts the concepts of effects and coeffects introduced in Section 2 to runtime mecha- nisms, constructing a theory of dynamic composition. The central idea is to turn the typing contexts carrying effects and coeffects into context types, i.e., runtime-operable types that reify the context as a first-class entity. For the effect type, we model it as a context transformation paired with an inverse, achieving local temporal composability. For the coeffect context, we model it as a type carrying dependency information, achieving local spatial composability. An observational equivalence on the coeffects then supplies the effects with independence. The unified context that carries both effects and coeffects constitutes a programming paradigm in its own right.', 'section': 'Revertible Effects and Reactive Coeffects', 'sec_num': '3'}, {'text': 'Temporal composability is the ability to load and unload components at runtime such that, upon unloading, the shared environment is recovered to its pre-composition state. This requires that every modification a component makes to the environment be both trackable and recoverable.', 'section': 'Revertible Effects', 'sec_num': '3.1'}, {'text': 'We therefore model an effect as a function of type Γ → Γ × (Γ → Γ): applied to the current context, it yields the modified context together with an explicit inverse. Supplying that inverse is what lets the effect be reverted, and returning it to the runtime is what makes the effect trackable. We call such effects revertible: by tracking and composing these inverses during execution, complete environment recovery becomes a structural guarantee.', 'section': 'Revertible Effects', 'sec_num': '3.1'}, {'text': 'Given any impure function 𝑓impure : 𝑋 → 𝑌 , we transform it into a pure form 𝑓 : Γ × 𝑋 → Γ × 𝑌 , where Γ is the context and all possible side effects can be represented as transformations on Γ. For any fixed input 𝑥 : 𝑋, the induced map 𝛾 ↦ pr1(𝑓(𝛾, 𝑥)) captures the side effect of 𝑓 independently of the return value. Effects on Γ therefore live in the monoid of transformations Γ → Γ under composition ∘, where each monoid axiom has a direct reading as a property of effects:', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': '• Closure: the sequential composition of two effects is again an effect; • Associativity: a composite effect is independent of how it is bracketed; • Identity: idΓ, the identity function on Γ, acts as the unit of composition.', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': 'To model effects that can be undone, we pair each transformation 𝑓 with another transfor- mation 𝑔 that undoes 𝑓, and call 𝑔 a left inverse of 𝑓, abbreviated to inverse throughout the paper.', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': 'Undoing is one-sided: what an inverse is held to is 𝑔 ∘ 𝑓 and never 𝑓 ∘ 𝑔. Pairs of transformations carry a multiplication of their own:', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': 'Definition 1. Define the twisted composition of pairs of context transformations by (𝑓1, 𝑔1) ∘ (𝑓2, 𝑔2) ≔ (𝑓1 ∘ 𝑓2, 𝑔2 ∘ 𝑔1) (4) As for ∘ itself, the left operand acts after the right, and the inverses accumulate in the opposite order. It makes (Γ → Γ) × (Γ → Γ) a monoid with unit (idΓ, idΓ), the product of the monoid of transformations with its opposite, which we call the twisted composition monoid 𝔗Γ over Γ.', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': 'To track effects within the context itself, we introduce the following definition:', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': 'Definition 2. Given a context Γ, define its effect context as: 𝜕Γ ≔ Γ × (Γ → Γ) (5) It can be understood as a pair (𝛾, 𝜑), where:', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': '• 𝛾 : Γ is the current context state; • 𝜑 : Γ → Γ is the accumulator, the composite of the inverses of the effects performed so far, and the function that recovers the context to its initial state.', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': 'In particular, the initial effect context can be represented as (𝛾0, idΓ).', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': 'We also write 𝜕2Γ = 𝜕Γ × (𝜕Γ → 𝜕Γ), and so on up the tower.', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': 'Given the presence of the accumulator 𝜑, all effects performed on 𝜕Γ can be tracked and recovered. We now give the concrete constructions for tracking and recovery.', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': 'Definition 3. Define the transformation trackΓ on pairs of context functions: trackΓ : (Γ → Γ) × (Γ → Γ) → 𝜕Γ → 𝜕Γ trackΓ = (𝑓, 𝑔) ↦ (𝛾, 𝜑) ↦ (𝑓(𝛾), 𝜑 ∘ 𝑔) (6) This transformation converts a forward function 𝑓 together with a candidate inverse 𝑔 into a transformation of the effect context 𝜕Γ. Applying trackΓ(𝑓, 𝑔) to a state (𝛾, 𝜑) transforms 𝛾 by 𝑓 and composes the inverse 𝑔 onto 𝜑, thereby tracking the effect of 𝑓 in the context.', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': 'Theorem 4. For every (𝑓, 𝑔) ∈ (Γ → Γ) × (Γ → Γ) the following diagram commutes, that is, pr1 ∘ trackΓ(𝑓, 𝑔) = 𝑓 ∘ pr1 (7) 𝑓 𝑓′ pr1 pr1track Γ Γ 𝜕Γ 𝜕Γ Proof. For all (𝛾, 𝜑) ∈ 𝜕Γ:', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': '(pr1 ∘ trackΓ(𝑓, 𝑔))(𝛾, 𝜑) = pr1(𝑓(𝛾), 𝜑 ∘ 𝑔) = 𝑓(𝛾) = (𝑓 ∘ pr1)(𝛾, 𝜑) □ Theorem 5. trackΓ is a monoid homomorphism from 𝔗Γ into 𝜕Γ → 𝜕Γ. That is, 1. trackΓ(idΓ, idΓ) = id𝜕Γ; 2. for all (𝑓1, 𝑔1), (𝑓2, 𝑔2) ∈ 𝔗Γ, trackΓ((𝑓1, 𝑔1) ∘ (𝑓2, 𝑔2)) = trackΓ(𝑓1, 𝑔1) ∘ trackΓ(𝑓2, 𝑔2) (8) Proof.', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': '1. The unit is carried to the unit, since trackΓ(idΓ, idΓ)(𝛾, 𝜑) = (𝛾, 𝜑 ∘ idΓ) = (𝛾, 𝜑).', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': '2. For the multiplication, take any (𝛾, 𝜑) ∈ 𝜕Γ:', 'section': 'Effect Context', 'sec_num': '3.1.1'}, {'text': '(trackΓ(𝑓1, 𝑔1) ∘ trackΓ(𝑓2, 𝑔2))(𝛾, 𝜑) = trackΓ(𝑓1, 𝑔1)(𝑓2(𝛾), 𝜑 ∘ 𝑔2) = (𝑓1(𝑓2(𝛾)), 𝜑 ∘ 𝑔2 ∘ 𝑔1) = trackΓ(𝑓1 ∘ 𝑓2, 𝑔2 ∘ 𝑔1)(𝛾, 𝜑) □ Definition 6. Define the transformation recoverΓ on 𝜕Γ: recoverΓ : 𝜕Γ → 𝜕Γ recoverΓ = (𝛾, 𝜑) ↦ (𝜑(𝛾), idΓ) (9) This transformation applies the recovery function 𝜑 to the current state 𝛾 and resets 𝜑 to the identity. The engine takes two inputs: the stashed set (file URLs whose contents have changed since the last reload) and the externals set (modules that cannot be hot-replaced and instead trigger a full restart). Writing get_imports(url) for the modules that url directly imports, it classifies the changes’ dependency subgraph, marking each module accepted or declined:', 'section': 'Hot Module Replacement', 'sec_num': '5.2.2'}, {'text': 'Algorithm 8 Module classification 1 function classify(stashed, externals) 2 accepted ← stashed 3 declined ← externals 4 pending ← ⌀ 5 for url in stashed do', 'section': 'Hot Module Replacement', 'sec_num': '5.2.2'}, {'text': '6 pending ← pending ∪ (get_imports(url) ∖ (accepted ∪ declined)) 7 repeat 8 progress ← false 9 for url in pending do 10 if get_imports(url) ∩ accepted ≠ ⌀ then 11 accepted ← accepted ∪ {url} 12 pending ← pending ∖ {url} 13 progress ← true 14 else if get_imports(url) ⊆ declined then 15 declined ← declined ∪ {url} 16 pending ← pending ∖ {url} 17 progress ← true 18 else 19 pending ← pending ∪ (get_imports(url) ∖ (accepted ∪ declined)) 20 until not progress 21 declined ← declined ∪ pending 22 return (accepted, declined) Seeded with the imports of the stashed files, the fixed point accepts a module once one of its imports is accepted and declines one once all of its imports are declined; any module left undecided, caught in an import cycle, defaults to declined.', 'section': 'Hot Module Replacement', 'sec_num': '5.2.2'}, {'text': 'Phase 2: Stale-entry detection. Finally, the engine reloads the stale entries. Over four years of development, it has accumulated over 4000 community-contributed plugins 5, ranging from instant-messaging (IM) adapters and database drivers to administrative consoles and end- user features. Its scale and diversity make it a representative validation of Cordis’s dynamic composability in a production setting.', 'section': 'Case Study: Koishi', 'sec_num': '5.3'}, {'text': 'Expressiveness and generality of the meta-framework. Koishi runs as a server-side bot whose every feature is realized as a plugin over the context primitives of Section 5.1; Koishi itself contributes only the chatbot-domain vocabulary. The same model reappears in a wholly different runtime: Koishi’s web console is a second, independent Cordis application whose plugins compose the primitives of the browser and its user interface rather than those of the server. The disparate settings above establish two properties of the model of Section 3. (1) It is expressive: its primitives suffice to carry a complete production system, the host framework supplying only domain vocabulary. (2) It is general: it fixes how effects and coeffects compose while leaving their meaning to each application, and so presupposes neither a particular domain nor a particular runtime.', 'section': 'Case Study: Koishi', 'sec_num': '5.3'}, {'text': 'Temporal composability without cognitive overhead. The plugin systems surveyed in Section 1.2.1 cannot unload an individual extension’s effects without restarting the extension 3On Node.js, this means clearing the caches of both the ES module and CommonJS module systems, since a module imported through the ES loader can appear in both. 4Koishi currently uses Cordis v3. This paper presents Cordis v4, which refines the effect and coeffect semantics and redesigns the loader; the core compositional model is shared across both versions. 5Koishi uses the term plugin for the concept this paper formalizes as component.', 'section': 'Case Study: Koishi', 'sec_num': '5.3'}, {'text': 'host. Koishi routinely performs this operation: an orchestrator disables a plugin from the console and its effects are withdrawn in place; during development, the HMR engine re-applies edited plugins on save while preserving cache state and live connections elsewhere in the system. Cordis makes such removal not merely possible but effortless for the plugin author.', 'section': 'Case Study: Koishi', 'sec_num': '5.3'}, {'text': 'Because effects performed through the context are tracked and their inverses composed auto - matically (Section 3.1), even an inexperienced author obtains ordered cleanup for a plugin’s context-mediated effects without writing an uninstall path. This achieves the locality of concern whose absence Section 1.2.1 identifies: correctness that would otherwise rest on each author’s diligence is instead discharged once, by the abstraction.', 'section': 'Case Study: Koishi', 'sec_num': '5.3'}, {'text': 'Spatial composability across an open ecosystem. In contrast to the plugin systems of Section 1.2.1, where inter-plugin dependencies are largely absent, Koishi’s ecosystem exhibits a genuine dependency topology: IM adapters provide access to each messaging platform, database drivers provide persistent storage, and functional plugins declare these as coeffects and access them. Reconfiguring a provider at runtime, such as switching the storage backend or reconnecting an adapter, reactivates only the dependents whose resolved dependency changed (Section 3.2); a plugin whose dependency is unavailable stays inactive until it appears, without erroring. What the case study substantiates is that this composition holds across independently authored code: a plugin and its dependencies are typically written by different authors who coordinate on nothing beyond the coeffect that connects them, so reactive coeffects keep the assembly consistent across an open ecosystem of independent contributors.', 'section': 'Case Study: Koishi', 'sec_num': '5.3'}, {'text': 'Threats to validity. The evidence here is drawn from a single ecosystem in a single host lan- guage, so it cannot separate the merits of the paradigm from those of its TypeScript realization or of Koishi’s particular domain, and it is observational rather than a controlled comparison against an alternative architecture. What the case study establishes is thus an existence-and- adoption result rather than a quantitative one; measuring the abstraction’s overhead and its effect on developer productivity against a baseline remains future work.', 'section': 'Case Study: Koishi', 'sec_num': '5.3'}, {'text': 'The formal model and implementation presented in the preceding sections introduce a programming paradigm for dynamic composability. This section examines how the paradigm extends to broader engineering concerns, and discusses the design tensions and open prob - lems.', 'section': 'Discussion', 'sec_num': '6'}, {'text': 'Every effect in Section 3.1 carries an inverse, and what that inverse amounts to is settled by the system boundary. The boundary divides the environment a system runs against into two parts.', 'section': 'System Boundary', 'sec_num': '6.1'}, {'text': '(1) A location lies inside when the system is able to modify it exclusively and to restore the state before that modification, so an operation on it is tracked in Γ and can be recovered later. (2) A location lies outside when either ability fails, so an operation on it acts as idΓ and is therefore neither tracked nor recovered. This section develops the properties of this boundary and their consequences for recovery.', 'section': 'System Boundary', 'sec_num': '6.1'}, {'text': 'Boundaries from coeffects. A coeffect moves the boundary by reifying an external location: it confines every access to that location to a set of operations it provides, each of which it can supply an inverse for, so operations that acted as idΓ come to be tracked in Γ and recovered. The', 'section': 'System Boundary', 'sec_num': '6.1'}, {'text': 'boundary is therefore drawn per location rather than per medium, since both aforementioned abilities are properties of a location, and reification changes how a location is accessed while leaving its medium as it was. For example, a memory region lies inside when the system alone writes it, and outside when other processes write it too; a file lies inside when only the system can reach it, as with a scratch file under a private path, and outside when it is a path other programs read or write. Moving the boundary is itself a trade-off, between whether the environment provides revertible semantics for a location and what supplying those semantics costs on every access. The record itself is part of the coeffect that reifies the location, e.g. an entry in a map it keeps, and installing that entry is a revertible effect. That record is at the same time the channel along which data can leave. (2) In the emission stage, the operation pushes data through that channel, as with the bytes a write hands to the file or the datagram a send puts on the wire, and the push acts as idΓ, leaving the data where other parties may read and write it. The two stages therefore fall on opposite sides of the boundary: the acquisition stays inside it, whereas the emission crosses to the outside.', 'section': 'System Boundary', 'sec_num': '6.1'}, {'text': 'Withholding and compensation. The metatheory does not: the commutation of Definition 60 is proved against ≃ and has to be re-established against the coarser one.', 'section': 'System Boundary', 'sec_num': '6.1'}, {'text': 'Dynamic component platforms such as OSGi [50] organize composition around services: units of functionality that a provider publishes under an interface and a consumer binds to. Components that provide a service are its providers, and components that inject a service are its consumers. A single service may be implemented by multiple providers, and this multiplicity can be realized in two forms. (1) Exclusive binding: several implementations share one interface but at most one is bound at a time; the orchestrator selects which implementation is bound, and switching between them requires unloading one provider and loading another, momentarily perturbing every consumer’s dependency. (2) Service broker : a central service that acts as the entrypoint for the interface is injected by both the backing providers and the consumers, so that multiple providers coexist and the broker dispatches each request among them. Compared to exclusive binding, the broker absorbs this perturbation: updating a backing provider leaves the broker in place, so consumers see no change to their dependency and no reload is triggered.', 'section': 'Service Multiplexing', 'sec_num': '6.2'}, {'text': 'The service broker underlies three capabilities: load balancing, rolling updates, and cross- process invocation.', 'section': 'Service Multiplexing', 'sec_num': '6.2'}, {'text': 'Load balancing. When several providers coexist, the broker distributes requests among them according to a configurable policy (e.g., round-robin, least-loaded, latency-weighted) or', 'section': 'Service Multiplexing', 'sec_num': '6.2'}, {'text': 'an explicit target named by the consumer. Because providers are ordinary components, they can be added or removed to scale capacity up or down; each provider registers with the broker through a revertible effect, so unloading it reverts the registration and drops it from the broker’s routing set automatically.', 'section': 'Service Multiplexing', 'sec_num': '6.2'}, {'text': 'Rolling updates. Upgrading a service implementation at runtime reduces to a controlled provider transition [51, 52]. To carry out the transition, the new provider is loaded as an additional fiber and registers with the broker; once it becomes ACTIVE, traffic is gradually shifted from the old providers to the new one (e.g., by adjusting selection weights), and the old providers are unloaded once they no longer carry in-flight requests. This provider transition turns what is traditionally an infrastructure-level operation (e.g., container orchestration, blue- green deployment) into an application-level composition pattern.', 'section': 'Service Multiplexing', 'sec_num': '6.2'}, {'text': 'Cross-process invocation. The service broker can also be applied across process boundaries [53]. Each process hosts its own Cordis context with local providers; a coordinating compo - nent links them, treating each as a remote provider. Cross-process service access is mediated by an RPC mechanism that preserves the interface, making the distribution transparent to consumers. One caveat is that a cross-process call incurs latency and may fail mid-flight, so exposing it synchronously would block the caller. An interface intended to be exposed across processes must therefore be designed against an asynchronous contract.', 'section': 'Service Multiplexing', 'sec_num': '6.2'}, {'text': 'Given an application assembled from independent components, securing the application calls for two complementary mechanisms: (1) constraining what dependencies a component may access, and (2) sandboxing untrusted code from the host environment. Since these requests are declared statically, the complete set of proxy-mediated capabilities a component requires is known before it runs, letting the orchestrator review and approve them at load time rather than discovering accesses as they happen.', 'section': 'Access Control and Sandboxing', 'sec_num': '6.3'}, {'text': 'This mediation generalizes to fine-grained policy through the interception mechanism.', 'section': 'Access Control and Sandboxing', 'sec_num': '6.3'}, {'text': 'Access-control metadata can be carried by contexts or declared by components (Definition 30), and the provider consults it when the dependency is invoked to decide whether a request is permitted. Because this interception lives on the context rather than in either party’s code, an orchestrator can adjust it to constrain any component’s access to a dependency without modifying the provider, e.g., granting read-only database access to a community component whereas a core component retains full access. A monolithic design would make each component depend on the other. However, the two interaction directions are logi - cally independent concerns. The two are complementary rather than competing: a Cordis coeffect can itself carry reactive values, and a component updates on only the parts it actually consumes, refining component-level reactivity into finer-grained reactive coeffects that span both levels.', 'section': 'Spatial Composability', 'sec_num': '7.4'}, {'text': 'We have presented a formal foundation for dynamic composability by lifting the classical concepts of effects and coeffects to runtime mechanisms. Revertible effects address local temporal composability: every context transformation carries an inverse that the runtime tracks, and both tracking and recovery preserve composition, so the context is recovered upon component removal. We unify the effect context and the coeffect context into a single context type, in which an observational equivalence on the coeffects supplies the effects with independence, constituting a programming paradigm for spatiotem - poral composability. Such validation would demonstrate the paradigm’s applicability as a foundation for recoverable, coordinated, and continuous self-evolution in agent harnesses and other autonomous systems.', 'section': 'Conclusion', 'sec_num': '8'}], 'back_matter': '[1] D. ## Overview of the plan
We have a clear mandate: the paper has no public reference implementation, so we must reimplement the Cordis meta-framework and validate the formal claims through property-based tests and a small plugin ecosystem harness. The paper itself contains no numeric benchmark suite; its main evidence is (1) the formal metatheory and (2) the Koishi production case study. Therefore, “reproducing the experiments” means:

1. Rebuilding the runtime machinery exactly enough to satisfy the paper’s stated invariants.
2. Constructing synthetic and semi-realistic component/plugin scenarios that exercise temporal composability, spatial composability, hot module replacement, and failure recovery.
3. Where possible, connecting the implementation to a proof-oriented model (or at least a precise executable specification) so the metatheorems can be checked.

Below is a step-by-step reproduction plan.

---

## 1. Guiding Goal and Overall Strategy

We will implement a TypeScript (Node.js) package mirroring the architecture of Cordis:

- **Core library**: `ctx.effect`, `ctx.get`, `ctx.set`, `ctx.isolate`, `ctx.intercept`, fiber lifecycle, reactive refresh, proxy-mediated context access.
- **Component loader**: declarative configuration entries, reconciliation, managed realms.
- **Hot module replacement**: module classification, stale-entry detection, transactional reload.

The implementation will be written from scratch, but every algorithm will follow the paper’s pseudocode (Algorithms 1–10) and the formal state machine in Section 4.

Because the paper is a *meta-framework* rather than an end-user application, we also need a deliberately small but realistic plugin suite to validate the system. We will use Koishi-style fixtures: database-provider plugins, message-adapter plugins, middleware plugins, and configuration panels.

---

## 2. Methodology Reconstruction

### 2.1 Formal Core to Reproduce

The paper is built on two symmetric abstractions:

- **Revertible effects** (Section 3.1). Every effect is a context transformation paired with an inverse. The runtime tracks the inverse and composes it onto an accumulator. Key types:
  - `𝔈Γ = Γ → Γ × (Γ → Γ)`
  - `𝔈*Γ` adds the witness condition `g(δ) = γ`.
  - `𝔈iterΓ` supports multi-step effects with a continuation.
  - `effectΓ` lifts an effect to the `∂Γ` level.
  - `trackΓ` and `recoverΓ` implement tracking/recovery.

- **Reactive coeffects** (Section 3.2). The context is a finite partial map `Σ = (k : K) ⇀ V k`. Components declare a dependency set `d`. The runtime classifies every domain change as `activating`, `deactivating`, or `neutral`. Additional structure:
  - `get`, `set` operations.
  - Isolation realms: `Σiso = (K ⇀ R) × ((r : R) ⇀ V r)`.
  - Interception metadata: `Σinter = ((k : K) → M k) × ((k : K) ⇀ (M k → V k))`.

- **Unified context** (Section 3.3): `Γ∞ = µΓ. Γ × (Γ → Γ) × Σ`.
  This is implemented as the `ctx` object carrying:
  - the current context state,
  - the accumulated dispose function,
  - the coeffect store / realm table / interception metadata.

- **Component and fiber model** (Section 4). A component is `(d, p, e)`:
  - `d`: declared dependencies,
  - `p`: declared provisions,
  - `e`: witnessed effect iterator.
  A fiber adds runtime state:
  - parent pointer,
  - local coeffect table,
  - retirement flag,
  - lifecycle state `Inactive | Reloading | Active | Unloading`.

- **Lifecycle rules**. The implementation must realize the ten rules:
  - Orchestration: `O-Insert`, `O-Retire`, `O-Remove`.
  - Activation: `L-Begin`, `L-Iter`, `L-Finish`.
  - Deactivation / interruption: `L-Leave`, `L-Unload`, `L-Divert`, `L-Raise`.

- **Target view and quiescence**. Every fiber computes a target view:
  - `target(γ,n) = ⊥` if retired or dependencies unsatisfied,
  - otherwise a map from declared keys to provider fiber UIDs.
  The system is quiescent when every fiber has reached its target.

- **Guarded deactivation**. A fiber cannot run its unload inverse until every fiber that depends on one of its provided keys has deactivated. This is the crucial ordering principle.

### 2.2 Implementation-Level Concepts to Reproduce

We need the following executable counterparts.

| Theory | Runtime (paper name) |
|---|---|
| `Γ∞` | `ctx` |
| `𝔈iterΓ` | callback passed to `ctx.effect` |
| `effectΓ(e)` | `ctx.effect(callback)` returning `dispose` |
| `Σ`, `Σiso`, `Σinter` | `ctx[@@store]`, `ctx[@@isolate]`, `ctx[@@intercept]` |
| `get(k)`, `set(k,v)` | `ctx.get(key)`, `ctx.set(key, value)` |
| `isolate(k,r)` | `ctx.isolate(key, realm?)` |
| `intercept(k,ν)` | `ctx.intercept(key, metadata)` |
| fiber | object returned by `ctx.use(component, config)` |
| `d`, `p`, `e` | `fiber.inject`, component’s `provide`, `fiber.apply` |
| accumulator `g` | `fiber.dispose` |
| committed view `ω` | `fiber.committed` |
| target view | `fiber.target`, recomputed by `refresh` |
| `O-Insert`, `O-Retire` | `ctx.use` callback and returned inverse |
| `L-Begin`, `L-Iter`, `L-Finish` | `reload` task |
| `L-Leave` | `refresh` marking fiber `UNLOADING` |
| `L-Unload` | `unload` task with dependent draining |
| guard on L-Unload | `await all(notify(...))` in `unload` |
| failure `L-Raise` | fiber state `FAILED`, target set to `⊥` |

## 3. Implementation Plan

We will implement Cordis in TypeScript with careful separation:

- `packages/core` — effect/coeffect primitives, fiber lifecycle.
- `packages/loader` — declarative configuration, reconciliation, managed realms.
- `packages/hmr` — hot module replacement engine.
- `packages/test-kit` — synthetic plugin fixtures, property-based testing utilities.

### Phase 0: Executable Specification / Type-Level Model

Before writing runtime code, we will encode the formal model as TypeScript types and a lightweight runtime verifier. This does not prove theorems, but it gives us a precise executable skeleton.

We will define:

```ts
type Key = string | symbol;
type Context = any; // loose initial representation
type EffectIterator = () => AsyncGenerator<Inverse, void, unknown>;
type Inverse = () => void | Promise<void>;
type CoeffectSpec = Set<Key>;
type Provision = Set<Key>;
```

We will formalize:

- `fiber.state` as a discriminated union matching Section 4.3:
  - `INACTIVE`
  - `LOADING`
  - `ACTIVE`
  - `UNLOADING`
  - `FAILED`

- `fiber.committed`: `Map<Key, FiberUID>`.
- `fiber.target`: `Map<Key, FiberUID> | null`.

We will also add development-only invariant checks:

- A fiber’s `dispose` must run exactly once.
- `fiber.committed` is constant while `ACTIVE`.
- A `UNLOADING` fiber provides no keys to new dependents.
- No two active fibers provide the same realm-resolved key.

### Phase 1: Core Context and Revertible Effects

**Goal:** implement `ctx.effect`.

The paper’s Algorithm 1 is the heart. We will implement:

1. **`execute(callback, guard)`**:
   - Call `callback()` to obtain an iterator.
   - Loop:
     - Check `guard()`; if false, break.
     - `await iterator.next()`.
     - If the yielded value is an inverse, compose it onto the accumulator in reverse order (`inverse = yieldedInverse ∘ inverse`).
     - If `done`, break.
   - Return the composite inverse.

2. **`effect(ctx, callback)`**:
   - Create an `armed` flag.
   - Start `execute(callback, () => armed)`.
   - `dispose()`:
     - If not armed, return.
     - Set `armed = false`.
     - Wait for the task to resolve.
     - Call the returned inverse.
     - Prepend this dispose onto `ctx.dispose`.

Important detail: if the callback is a *plain* function returning a single inverse rather than an iterator, we adapt it to an iterator with one step. This matches the paper’s statement that `ctx.effect` accepts both `𝔈Γ` and `𝔈iterΓ`.

**Tests for Phase 1**:
- A `ctx.effect` that mutates a value and returns a restoring inverse leaves the context unchanged after `dispose()`.
- Multiple effects composed sequentially are disposed in LIFO order.
- A partially executed generator can be interrupted by clearing `armed`; only already-performed steps are undone.
- A `dispose()` is idempotent.

### Phase 2: Coeffect Store

**Goal:** implement `ctx.get`, `ctx.set`, `ctx.isolate`, `ctx.intercept`.

We will maintain:

- `ctx[@@store]`: a `Map<RealmSymbol, unknown>` from realm symbols to values.
- `ctx[@@isolate]`: a `Map<Key, RealmSymbol>`.
- `ctx[@@intercept]`: a `Map<Key, Metadata>`.

#### `ctx.get(key)`

1. Resolve `realm = ctx[@@isolate].get(key)`; if absent, use `key` itself as realm.
2. Return `ctx[@@store].get(realm)`.

#### `ctx.set(key, value)`

1. Return `ctx.effect(callback)`.
2. Inside callback:
   - Resolve realm.
   - Write `ctx[@@store].set(realm, value)`.
   - Call `notify(ctx, [key])`.
   - Return the inverse: delete the store entry and `notify(ctx, [key])` again.

This matches Algorithm 2.

#### `ctx.isolate(key, realm?)`

- If realm not provided, create a fresh `Symbol()`.
- Derive a child context (or mutate a dedicated child context) so that `@@isolate` maps `key` to the new realm.
- Since this derives a context rather than mutating the store, no inverse is tracked.

#### `ctx.intercept(key, metadata)`

- Merge metadata into `ctx[@@intercept]` according to the key’s metadata monoid.
- In TypeScript, we will implement a default “right-biased merge” but allow components to supply a custom merge function.

#### `notify(ctx, keys)` (Algorithm 3)

- For every live fiber:
  - If the key is in `fiber.inject` and the fiber’s own context resolves that key to the same realm as the changed context, call `refresh(fiber)`.
- Return the set of fibers that were refreshed.

**Crucial subtlety:** `notify` must be called on the *parent context* of the provider, but a dependent can have an isolated realm. The implementation must compare realms via `fiber.ctx[@@isolate][key]`, not by key equality. We will store `fiber.ctx` as a derived child context.

### Phase 3: Fiber Lifecycle

**Goal:** implement `ctx.use(component, config)` and the lifecycle state machine.

#### Component object

Each component provides:

- `inject`: `readonly Key[]`
- `provide`: `readonly Key[]` (or derivable from `apply` effects; paper requires explicit)
- `apply(ctx, config)`: an effect callback or iterator.

#### `ctx.use`

Follow Algorithm 4:

```ts
function use(ctx, component, config) {
  const fiber = new Fiber(parentCtx: ctx, inject: component.inject);
  fiber.ctx = deriveChildContext(ctx, fiber);
  fiber.apply = () => component.apply(fiber.ctx, config);

  const callback = async () => {
    refresh(fiber);
    return () => {
      fiber.target = null;
      unload(fiber);
    };
  };

  ctx.effect(callback);
  return fiber;
}
```

This makes instantiation a tracked effect of the parent context, enabling cascaded unload.

#### `refresh(fiber)`

Implement `target(γ, n)` per Definition 46:

- If `fiber.retired` or any declared key is not provided by an *Active* fiber, target = `null`.
- Otherwise, target = `Map<Key, UID>` where each key maps to the UID of the active provider.

Then:

```ts
function refresh(fiber) {
  const newTarget = computeTarget(fiber);
  if (newTarget === fiber.target) return;
  fiber.target = newTarget;

  if (fiber.inertia) return; // inertial transition in progress

  if (newTarget !== null) {
    fiber.state = LOADING;
    fiber.inertia = schedule(reload(fiber));
  } else {
    fiber.state = UNLOADING;
    fiber.inertia = schedule(unload(fiber));
  }
}
```

#### `reload(fiber)`

Per Algorithm 5:

```ts
async function reload(fiber) {
  const target0 = fiber.target;
  fiber.committed = resolve(fiber.inject);

  const recover = await execute(fiber.apply, () => fiber.target === target0);
  fiber.dispose = compose(recover, fiber.dispose);

  if (fiber.target === target0) {
    fiber.state = ACTIVE;
    notify(fiber.ctx, provided(fiber));
    fiber.inertia = null;
  } else {
    fiber.state = UNLOADING;
    fiber.inertia = schedule(unload(fiber));
  }
}
```

This ensures the fiber only becomes ACTIVE if its resolution did not change during activation.

#### `unload(fiber)`

Per Algorithm 5:

```ts
async function unload(fiber) {
  const dependents = notify(fiber.ctx, provided(fiber));
  await Promise.all(dependents.map(d => d.awaitQuiescence()));
  await fiber.dispose();
  fiber.dispose = id;
  fiber.committed = null;

  if (fiber.target === null) {
    fiber.state = INACTIVE;
    fiber.inertia = null;
  } else {
    fiber.state = LOADING;
    fiber.inertia = schedule(reload(fiber));
  }
}
```

**Crucial:** `notify` inside unload must mark dependents as UNLOADING *before* `fiber.dispose` runs. This is the guard from Section 4.3.1.

We will implement `fiber.awaitQuiescence()` as a helper that resolves when the fiber reaches INACTIVE (or FAILED).

#### Error handling

If `execute` throws or the iterator yields a failure, catch it inside `reload`, set a fiber error state:

```ts
fiber.state = FAILED;
fiber.target = null;
fiber.inertia = null;
```

Tracking is still recovered because the accumulator built so far is applied in an L-Raise-style path.

### Phase 4: Proxy-Mediated Context Access

Per Algorithm 6, `ctx[key]` should resolve against the accessing fiber’s committed view:

- Walk up from `ctx.fiber` through `parent.fiber`.
- If a fiber’s committed view has `key`, return the bound provider’s value.
- If a fiber declares `key` but has no committed view, throw `INACTIVE_ACCESS`.
- If root is reached, throw `UNDECLARED_ACCESS`.

Implementation detail: we need to know which fiber is accessing the context. We will attach a hidden `fiber` property to every derived context, and use a `Proxy` on the context. Components should use `ctx.foo` for declared dependencies; raw `ctx.get` remains available as an escape hatch.

We will also export a function to provision values with proper typing, e.g., `ctx.provide(key, value)` syntactic sugar for `ctx.set`.

### Phase 5: Component Loader and Declarative Configuration

The loader should translate a configuration tree into fiber operations.

#### Configuration entry

```ts
interface Entry {
  id: string;
  url: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
  isolate?: boolean | string; // per-key or global?
  intercept?: Record<string, unknown>;
  config?: unknown;
  children?: Entry[]; // for group/include
}
```

#### Reconciliation

When an entry changes, apply the least disruptive operation:

- `id` or `url` changed → dispose old fiber, create new fiber.
- `disabled` set true → retire and unload fiber.
- `disabled` set false → ensure fiber is loaded.
- `isolate` changed → patch the realm table and reload only the affected fiber(s).
- `intercept` changed → mutate metadata; no reload.
- `config` changed → pass the new config into the component’s `apply`.

For group entries, use keyed diff over child ids and recurse.

#### Managed realms

Implement `patch_isolation(entry, newIsolation)` from Algorithm 7:

- Determine keys whose realm changed.
- Write a fresh delimiter symbol `δ_k` on the entry’s context.
- Capture old realm, new realm, entry tag, provider tag.
- Update `entry.ctx[@@isolate]`.
- Reload the entry’s fiber.
- Move the stored binding from old realm to new realm if the entry is the provider (delimiter tags match).
- Call a specialized `notify` that filters fibers by delimiter tags.

This is one of the trickiest parts because realm scope is dynamic. We will build a small abstract “context derivation tree” to make delimiter inheritance explicit.

### Phase 6: Hot Module Replacement

Implement Algorithms 8, 9, and 10.

#### Module graph

We need an import graph. In Node.js, this can be approximated with static analysis of `import`/`require` statements, or more robustly by hooking the module loader. To stay independent of bundlers, we will implement a simple dependency scanner supporting relative paths and node_modules resolution.

#### Classification

For a set of changed files and external non-replaceable modules:

- Start with `accepted = stashed`, `declined = externals`.
- Compute transitive imports.
- Fixed point:
  - if a pending module imports an accepted module, accept it;
  - if all its imports are declined, decline it;
  - otherwise keep pending and add its unseen imports.
- Default remaining pending modules to declined.

#### Stale entry detection

For every configuration entry, collect transitive dependencies that do not cross declined boundaries. If the tree intersects accepted modules, mark the entry stale and add its whole tree to accepted.

#### Transactional reload

- Clear module caches for accepted modules.
- Back up the previous component modules.
- For each stale entry, dispose its fiber and create a new fiber from the freshly imported module.
- On any error:
  - restore caches from backup,
  - dispose all partially replaced fibers,
  - re-create fibers from backup component modules,
  - rethrow.

We will implement on Node.js using `require.cache` clearing for CommonJS and an internal `module` registry for ESM; for a pure Vite/Webpack environment, the same logic maps to `import.meta.hot`.

## 4. Experimental Validation

### 4.1 Property-Based Test Suite

We will use `fast-check` (or `vitest` + custom property runners) to validate the metatheorems on small random component graphs.

#### Temporal composability

Define an observable context equivalence `≃` for tests:

- Two states are equivalent if:
  - the coeffect projections bind the same keys;
  - for each key, values are deep-equal, or equal according to a custom key equivalence.

Property tests:

1. **Recovery exactness**:
   - Load a fiber.
   - Run a random interleaving of operations from *other* fibers.
   - Unload the original fiber.
   - The resulting state, up to control fields, equals the state that would result from applying the other fibers’ operations alone.

2. **LIFO inverse composition**:
   - A fiber with many effects yields inverses applied in reverse order.

3. **Interruption rollback**:
   - A fiber whose apply callback yields multiple iterations is interrupted mid-way (target changes).
   - Only the already-installed effects are reverted.

#### Spatial composability

1. **Activation ordering**:
   - A fiber with dependency `k` must not become ACTIVE before a fiber providing `k` is ACTIVE.

2. **Withdrawal ordering**:
   - When provider of `k` is retired, it must not run its inverse until all fibers with `committed[k] = provider` have reached INACTIVE.

3. **Resolution coherence**:
   - During a fiber’s transition from INACTIVE to ACTIVE, all iterations are executed against the same committed view.

4. **Replacement**:
   - Replacing a provider with another provider of the same key causes exactly the dependents to reload; irrelevant fibers do not reload.

#### Progress and Confluence

1. **No deadlock**:
   - From any non-quiescent state satisfying acyclicity of `≺` (`p_n ∩ d_m` relation), some lifecycle step is applicable.

2. **Termination**:
   - With finite fibers and bounded iteration lengths, starting from a valid configuration and applying orchestration steps, the system always reaches quiescence.

3. **Confluence**:
   - Given two different schedules (random orderings of lifecycle steps), the two final states are equivalent:
     - same active fibers,
     - same provided values,
     - same target/committed views up to UID renaming.

### 4.2 Synthetic Plugin Ecosystem

We will construct a mini “Koishi-like” ecosystem with:

- **Database provider plugin** — provides `db` coeffect.
- **Logger plugin** — provides `logger` coeffect.
- **Message adapter plugin** — provides `adapter` and depends on `db`, `logger`.
- **Command plugin** — depends on `adapter`, `db`, `logger`.
- **Admin console plugin** — depends on `adapter`, `db`; provides `admin`.
- **HMR test plugin** — a component whose module file is swapped during the test.

This lets us test realistic compositions:

- Startup order: command plugin should wait for adapter and db.
- Runtime replacement: swap database provider while command plugin is running.
- Runtime disable: disable command plugin; its effects vanish.
- Cascaded unload: disable adapter; command plugin and admin console unload first.
- Full reload via HMR: edit command plugin source; only command plugin reloads, while db and adapter stay alive.
- Transactional rollback: introduce a syntax error in a changed plugin; HMR restores previous plugin and leaves system running.

### 4.3 Evaluation Metrics

Because the paper does not claim performance superiority, our key metrics are *correctness and structural properties*:

- Number of property tests passed (`0` failures).
- Proportion of random schedules that reach a quiescent state (`100%` within finite bound).
- Number of invariant violations (should be `0`).
- Optional performance benchmarks:
  - overhead of `ctx.effect` vs direct function call;
  - memory retained after fiber unload;
  - time to reload a plugin on HMR;
  - time to reconcile a large synthetic configuration.

We will not claim to reproduce Koishi’s scale (4000+ plugins), but we will show that the architecture scales to hundreds of synthetic fibers in stress tests.

### 4.4 Formal Verification (Optional but Recommended)

If time permits, we will encode the core definitions in a proof assistant such as Agda, Coq, or Lean:

- effect contexts, twisted composition, `track`, `recover`,
- witnessed effect functions,
- reactive coeffect satisfaction,
- the transition system of Section 4.

This would let us mechanically check the central theorems:

- Theorem 7 (recovery),
- Theorem 16 (LIFO revert),
- Theorem 61 (recovery exactness),
- Theorem 63 (ordering),
- Theorem 73 (confluence).

A full formalization is heavy, but even a mechanized proof of the core monoid facts (`track` preserves composition, and inverse composition) would greatly increase confidence.

## 5. Unclear Points and Assumptions

The paper leaves several details underspecified for a concrete implementation. We will resolve them as follows:

1. **Realm symbols and delimiter semantics**  
   The paper says `δ_k` is a fresh tag and uses `store[s₁].fiber.ctx[δ_k]` to identify whether a binding “belongs” to an entry. We will implement this by giving every context a chain of delimiter maps. When deriving a child context, delimiters are inherited. A fresh tag is generated for each key on every realm reassignment.

2. **`target(γ, n)` exact computation**  
   The paper defines it conceptually, but not how to compute providers efficiently. We will maintain a reverse index from `(realm, key) -> fiberUID` for active fibers. `target` for a fiber then queries this index for each declared key.

3. **`provided(fiber)`**  
   Similarly, we need to know which keys a fiber provides. We will collect this from:
   - the `provide` set declared by the component, and
   - a runtime record of keys actually written to `fiber.ctx[@@store]`.
   The runtime record is safer because a component might not provide everything it declared. We will reconcile both.

4. **Async scheduling model**  
   The paper’s `create_task` is abstract. In TypeScript, we will use `Promise`-based scheduling, but to make race conditions testable we will expose a `scheduler` abstraction:
   - `schedule(task)` returns a handle.
   - `await all(...)` waits for handles.
   - Tests can force deterministic ordering by controlling the scheduler queue.

5. **Observational equivalence `≃`**  
   Section 3.3.2 defines state equivalence in terms of application-specific `≃_k`. For a generic TypeScript library, we cannot know the right equivalence for every value type. We will:
   - Default to `Object.is` / deep equality for plain data.
   - Allow components to provide a custom `equivalence(key)` hook.
   - Use this equivalence in tests and in dev-mode invariant checking.

6. **Commutativity checking**  
   Independence of effects is assumed, not checked. We will implement optional dev-mode warnings when two concurrently active fibers write to the same realm or when a key’s operations are known to be order-sensitive. The system cannot automatically verify commutativity.

7. **HMR module graph**  
   We will implement a conservative static scanner. For production, this would be replaced by bundler-specific hooks. The paper’s algorithm is generic, but real-world edge cases (dynamic imports, CSS imports, virtual modules) may require configuration.

8. **Type-level dependency declarations**  
   The paper describes runtime access checking and mentions that a host language could mediate at compile time. Since our target is TypeScript, we can use declaration merging or module augmentation so `ctx.get('db')` is typed when plugins declare their injections. This is peripheral to the formal model, but improves usability.

## 7. Final Deliverables

By the end of this reproduction, we should have:

- A working Cordis-compatible core library in TypeScript.
- A declarative loader with reconciliation and HMR.
- A robust test suite demonstrating:
  - temporal composability (clean unload and rollback),
  - spatial composability (dependency ordering and reactive reload),
  - progress and confluence (random schedule tests),
  - transactional HMR.
- Documentation explaining how each formal definition maps to code.
- Optional: a proof-of-concept formalization of the core effect algebra.

This plan gives us a direct path from the paper’s formal contributions to an executable, testable implementation. The key is to never lose sight of the paper’s central invariants: complete recovery on unload, dependency-driven activation/deactivation, guarded provider withdrawal, and schedule-independent quiescence.

# Logic Analysis: `src/effect.ts`

## 1. Role of the file

`src/effect.ts` implements **revertible effect tracking**, corresponding to:

- Paper **Algorithm 1** (Effect tracking)
- Paper **Section 3.1** (`track`, `recover`, `effectΓ`, `𝔈iterΓ`)
- Paper **Section 5.1.1** (`ctx.effect`)
- Configuration:
  - `core.effectTracking.executionModel: async-generator`
  - `core.effectTracking.inverseComposition: LIFO`
  - `core.effectTracking.armedGuard: true`
  - `core.effectTracking.guardCheckPerIteration: true`
  - `core.effectTracking.disposalIsIdempotent: true`

This file provides the **single mutation primitive** of the framework. All higher-level operations (`ctx.set`, `ctx.use`, component effects) eventually reduce to `EffectEngine.effect(ctx, callback)`.

---

## 2. Imports and dependency direction

`src/effect.ts` depends on:

- `./types` — for `Key`, `Dispose`, `Inverse`, `Guard`, `EffectCallback`, `Context` type reference.
- `./context` — for the `Context` class.

A circular dependency exists at runtime: `Context` delegates to `EffectEngine`, while `EffectEngine` only needs `Context` as a **type**. Therefore:

```ts
import type { Context } from './context';
```

This breaks the runtime cycle while still satisfying the design.

`EffectEngine` should not reach into private `Context` slots (`@@store`, `@@isolate`, `@@intercept`). It only needs the public `ctx.dispose` property.

## 4. `identity()`

`identity()` returns a no-op disposer:

```ts
static identity(): Dispose {
  return () => {};
}
```

It is the initial accumulator in `execute`.

It is also the reset value of `fiber.dispose` after unload.

---

## 5. `compose(a, b)` and the LIFO invariant

This is the most semantically important helper.

### Requirement

Given two disposers `a` and `b`, the returned disposer must preserve **LIFO recovery**:

- If an effect yields inverse `v1`, then later yields inverse `v2`,
- then running the final composite must run `v2` first, then `v1`.

### Chosen convention

We define:

```ts
compose(a, b) = async () => {
  await a();
  await b();
};
```

That is, **`a` runs first**.

This matches the LIFO usage:

```ts
inverse = compose(value, inverse);
```

where `value` is the newly yielded inverse and `inverse` is the previously accumulated one.

### Why this order is correct

- First yielded inverse: `inverse = compose(v1, identity)`
  - runs `v1`
- Second yielded inverse: `inverse = compose(v2, inverse)`
  - runs `v2`, then runs the previous composite, which runs `v1`

Result: `v2` before `v1`, i.e., **last-in-first-out**.

### Documenting the convention

The design text says `compose(a, b)` runs `b` before `a`. If that exact convention is kept internally, the call sites must be swapped:

```ts
inverse = compose(inverse, value);        // runs value first
ctx.dispose = compose(ctx.dispose, dispose); // runs dispose first
```

Either implementation is acceptable as long as the **observable LIFO order** is:

> Most recently registered inverse runs first.

The source of truth is the LIFO invariant, not the argument names.

---

## 6. Normalizing an `EffectCallback` to an async iterator

`EffectCallback` is:

```ts
() => AsyncGenerator<Inverse, void, unknown> | (() => Inverse | void)
```

`execute` must accept both forms.

### Cases

1. **Async generator returned**
   - The callback returns an object with `next()`, `return()`, `throw()`.
   - Use it directly.

2. **Plain disposer function returned**
   - The callback returns a function `() => void | Promise<void>`.
   - This is a single inverse.
   - Wrap it in a one-shot async generator:

```ts
async function* single(dispose: Dispose) {
  yield dispose;
}
```

3. **`undefined` / `null` returned**
   - Treat as an effect with no inverses.
   - Use an empty async generator.

4. **Sync generator returned** *(robustness)*
   - Not in the type, but can be supported by wrapping `next()` with `Promise.resolve`.

### Important distinction

- A **function** returned from `callback()` is treated as an **inverse/disposer**, not as another callback.
- An **object with `next`** is treated as an **iterator**.

This distinction matters when normalizing.

## 7. `execute(callback, guard)` — detailed algorithm

This is the engine that drives effect iteration.

### Steps

```text
1. If guard() is false:
   - return identity()
   - (Do not call callback() if no iteration should run.)

2. const result = callback()

3. Normalize result to an async iterator.

4. let inverse = identity()

5. while guard() is true:
   a. const step = await iterator.next()
   b. if step.done: break
   c. const value = step.value
   d. if typeof value === 'function':
        inverse = compose(value, inverse)
      else:
        // ignore non-function yields, or warn in dev mode
6. return inverse
```

### Guard semantics

- `guard` is checked **before each iteration**.
- This includes an initial check before `callback()` is invoked.
- The purpose is to enable **step-boundary interruption**:
  - If the target view changes between iterations,
  - only already-performed effects are kept,
  - remaining iterations are not executed.

### Why the initial guard check matters

For an async generator callback, calling `callback()` alone does not execute the body; side effects begin on the first `next()`.

For a plain disposer-style callback, side effects happen immediately when `callback()` is invoked. Therefore, checking `guard()` before calling `callback()` prevents applying an effect when the guard is already false.

In the lifecycle use case, this corresponds to `L-Divert` aborting before any new iteration runs.

### Handling yielded inverses

- A yielded `value` is a `Dispose` function.
- Only functions should be composed.
- `if (value)` from the paper is replaced by:

```ts
if (typeof value === 'function') {
  inverse = compose(value, inverse);
}
```

This avoids composing `0`, `''`, `false`, etc.

### Error behavior

- If `callback()` throws, `execute` rejects.
- If `iterator.next()` rejects, `execute` rejects.
- No inverse is manufactured for a failed iteration.
- `execute` does **not** swallow errors.
- Recovery of already-yielded inverses on failure is the responsibility of the caller (`Lifecycle.reload` / L-Raise path).

## 8. `effect(ctx, callback)` — public effect primitive

This wraps `execute` with:

- **armed guard**
- **idempotent disposal**
- **parent-context composition**

### Algorithm

```text
1. let armed = true

2. const task = execute(callback, () => armed)

3. function dispose():
   a. if not armed: return
   b. armed = false
   c. const recover = await task
   d. await recover()
   e. ctx.dispose = compose(dispose, ctx.dispose)

4. return dispose
```

### Idempotency

- `armed` starts `true`.
- The first call to `dispose()` sets it to `false`.
- Any later call returns immediately.
- This satisfies:

```yaml
disposalIsIdempotent: true
```

### Interaction with in-flight iteration

Suppose `dispose()` is called while `execute` is awaiting `iterator.next()`.

- `armed` becomes `false`.
- When the pending `next()` resolves, the loop checks `guard()`.
- It stops before the next iteration.
- The inverses already yielded are composed and returned by `task`.
- `dispose()` then awaits `task` and runs the composite inverse.

This is exactly **partial rollback**:

> A component effect interrupted mid-way is reverted as far as it has already progressed.

### Parent-context registration

After successful recovery:

```ts
ctx.dispose = compose(dispose, ctx.dispose);
```

This **prepends** the current effect’s disposer to the parent context accumulator.

Because `compose` runs the first argument first, disposing the parent context will dispose this effect before previously registered effects.

This gives cross-effect LIFO ordering:

- First created effect: registered first.
- Second created effect: registered before first.
- Parent disposal runs second’s disposer before first’s.

### When `recover()` throws

- `armed` is already `false`.
- The error propagates to the caller of `dispose()`.
- `ctx.dispose` is not extended, matching the paper’s sequential form:

```text
recover();
ctx.dispose = dispose ∘ ctx.dispose;
```

This should be documented as an assumption: inverses are expected to succeed.

## 9. Key invariants preserved by this file

### 9.1 LIFO within one effect

Given yielded inverses `v1, v2, ..., vn`, the returned composite performs:

```text
vn, then v(n-1), ..., then v1
```

### 9.2 LIFO across effects on one context

When multiple `ctx.effect` disposers are registered on the same `ctx.dispose`, the later-created effect is disposed first.

### 9.3 Guard checked per iteration

The loop cannot advance past an iteration unless the guard is true.

### 9.4 Disposal at most once

The `armed` flag guarantees that an effect’s inverse runs at most once.

### 9.5 No effect leakage

If a callback yields no inverses, `execute` returns `identity()`; disposal still completes safely.

---

## 10. Edge cases and decisions

### 10.1 Callback returns a plain function

```ts
ctx.effect(() => {
  // perform side effect
  return () => { /* undo */ };
});
```

In `execute`, the returned function is **not called immediately**. It is yielded as the inverse and will be called when the composite inverse runs.

### 10.2 Callback returns an async generator

```ts
ctx.effect(async function* () {
  yield undo1;
  yield undo2;
});
```

`execute` iterates it directly.

### 10.3 Callback returns `undefined`

This can happen if the callback has an early `return`.

`execute` treats it as an empty iterator. No inverse is recorded, but no crash occurs.

### 10.4 Generator completes without yielding

`inverse` remains `identity()`.

### 10.5 Guard becomes false during an awaited `next()`

The yielded value from that completed iteration is still composed, then the loop stops. This is correct: the iteration has already happened, so its inverse must be kept.

### 10.6 Non-function yield

The type says only `Dispose` values are yielded, but defensive code should check `typeof value === 'function'` before composing.

### 10.7 `dispose()` called twice

Second call is a no-op due to `armed === false`.

### 10.8 `dispose()` called before the first `next()` resolves

`armed` is set to `false`; the loop stops after the current or first iteration completes.

## 11. Relationship to the lifecycle

Although `src/effect.ts` does not define the fiber lifecycle, it is the engine used by `Lifecycle.reload`:

- `fiber.apply` is an `EffectCallback`.
- `Lifecycle.reload` calls:

```ts
EffectEngine.execute(fiber.apply, () => fiber.target === target0)
```

- The guard is the **target fixity check** from `Theorem 64`.
- The returned composite inverse is folded into `fiber.dispose`.

Thus this file is responsible for:

- executing component effects,
- collecting their inverses,
- enabling interruption at iteration boundaries,
- providing the raw inverse that unload will apply.

The lifecycle adds:

- committed view management,
- guarded withdrawal,
- state transitions.

`src/effect.ts` is a focused, single-responsibility module:

| Concern | Implementation |
|---|---|
| Effect iteration | `execute(callback, guard)` |
| LIFO inverse accumulation | `inverse = compose(value, inverse)` |
| Atomic tracked effect | `effect(ctx, callback)` |
| Idempotent disposal | `armed` flag |
| Parent-context registration | `ctx.dispose = compose(dispose, ctx.dispose)` |
| No-op disposer | `identity()` |
| Composite disposer | `compose(a, b)` |

The central invariant is:

> At every level — inside a single effect and across effects on one context — the most recently registered inverse runs first, and disposal is safe to call at most once.
